newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Ifo says sees 1997 German jobless at 10.9 pct.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Ifo says sees 1997 German jobless at 10.9 pct.

text.p: Germany's Ifo economic institute on Thursday painted a grim picture of the German labour market when it said that it expected jobless levels to reach 10.9 percent in 1997, up from 10.4 percent last year.

"The jobless rate will be, according to our estimates, 10.9 percent in 1997 and thus will continue to rise," Ifo President Karl Heinrich Oppenlaender at a conference on the economic implications of the euro currency.
But an improvement in economic growth would not be enough in itself to bring about an appreciable improvement in the employment situation.

Oppenlaender said growth "would have to be three to four percent to do anything about this situation," adding that he did not expect that Germany can achieve its stated goal of halving unemployment by the year 2000.
"I can not imagine this at all," he said.

German unemployment soared to a post-war record level of 4.66 million in January -- the highest level seen since the 1930's -- spawning a rash of worries that structural problems were sapping fuel from Europe's economic motor.

The surge in jobless numbers, which represents a drain on Bonn's budget, comes just as the government is making every effort to rein in spending to make the grade for Europe's economic and monetary union.

The Munich-based IFO institute said it expected 1997 pan-German real Gross Domestic Product growth of 2.5 percent compared with 1.4 percent in 1996 and for real private consumption to rise 1.5 percent during the year.
In addition, Ifo said it expected real growth of six percent in 1997 for German exports and that capital equipment expenditures would rise a real four percent during the year.

Oppenlaender said that the current upturn in the German economy would last at least until the end of 1997 and possibly until mid-1998. "I see this lasting one-and-a-half to two years, with the starting point at mid-1996," he told Reuters.
Ifo was not making detailed forecasts for 1998 because of uncertainties on whether planned tax reforms could be implemented in early 1998.
"Private consumption would certainly be given significant support," if they are implemented, he said.
Levels of investment were sluggish at the moment and this would have to change in an economic upswing.
Oppenlaender went on to say that the German state financing deficit would be about 120 billion marks this year, once again as a result of higher transfers to the developing east German states.
"The high jobless level and the high state financing deficit are urgent problems to be solved," Oppenlaender said.
He added that solutions must be found on wage policies, especially in east German states and a simultaneous change in budgetary conditions which would boost investment.

Oppenlaender said the German economy was generally being driven by foreign demand at a time when domestic demand was weakening. At the same time, investing in Germany had to be made attractive in the medium term for foreign investors.

He said east German states were "very far from a self-sufficient upswing" due to their uncompetitive position and said growth in 1997 in east German states would be lower than that in former West Germany for the first time since 1992.

Oppelaender said the outlook for private consumption had changed little and predicted growth in real private consumption of 1.5 percent for 1997. This forecast presumed a rise of 1.5 percent in pre-tax wages, he added.
